intro: The board compares surfaces and methods through contemporary exhibits. The traditions connect to custodians, places and histories that a small visual sample can only begin to introduce.
alt: Museum studies of painted bark, a dot-painted panel, a curved rafter design and patterned barkcloth.

variants.name: Aboriginal bark painting
variants.look: The bark's uneven edge remains visible beside earthy paint and crosshatched lines.
variants.history: Bark painting has long and varied histories. In Arnhem Land, artists in different communities paint on prepared eucalyptus bark and have distinctive responsibilities for designs and stories.
variants.when: Look at artist- or community-approved examples to study the relationship between a surface, paint and particular place.
variants.why: Bark changes the size and shape of the available surface, and patterns can have meanings held by specific people.

variants.name: Western Desert dot painting
variants.look: Separate touches of pigment form visible clusters and seams across the practice panel.
variants.history: Beginning in the early 1970s, artists at Papunya used commercial paints and portable supports. Western Desert artists continue to develop distinct ways to paint Country.
variants.when: Use public examples and their artist statements to study the movement within a painted field.
variants.why: Densely and loosely spaced dots can guide the eye. Their presence alone says little about who made a work or what it means.

variants.name: kōwhaiwhai
variants.look: Red, black and white curves bend and repeat along a beam.
variants.history: Māori kōwhaiwhai is painted ornament often found on rafters in meeting houses. Particular designs can carry associations with ancestry or place.
variants.when: Study documented examples when thinking about shape that follows an architectural length.
variants.why: A repeat along a beam lets a curve pull the viewer's eye through space.

source.label: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

variants.name: tapa cloth
variants.look: The brown repeat lies on a large sheet whose thin raw edge still shows its fibrous construction.
variants.history: Pacific barkcloth has many names and local techniques. Artisans beat prepared inner bark and may rub, stencil or paint patterns onto it.
variants.when: Look at public examples to compare where a pattern follows joins and where it runs across them.
variants.why: Beaten bark makes a wide, flexible surface without weaving individual threads.

source.label: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: public museum exhibit of northern Australian Aboriginal bark-painting technique, long visible eucalyptus bark edge and earth pigment crosshatching on a nonfigurative publicly shareable surface sample; Western Desert acrylic dot-painting technique neutral materials display with irregular colored dot marks only on a small abstract study, no sacred patterns; Māori kōwhaiwhai study of black, red and white painted curving forms on a timber beam, decorative public example; Pacific tapa barkcloth study with stenciled brown repeat pattern and unmistakable thin beaten bark edge. No invented ceremonies, sacred symbols, or person-as-maker. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
